note: The Hills Are Alive, level 1 mostly revealed by placing a lit party in each area.

view.adventure_description: The barrow-hills above the caravan town of Last Well have begun to sing: a thin, dry keening that rises from the sand at moonrise and stops at dawn. The oldest maps name the valley below the hills the Valley of Sleeping Kings, and the singing comes from its last unopened door — the House of the Second Dawn, tomb of Ozrum the Deathless, a god-king who was promised he would rise when a second dawn broke inside his burial vault. His vizier Uzhep went into the tomb with him, alive, to arrange it. The town wants the singing stopped before whatever practices dawn down there finishes rehearsing.
view.town_description: A caravan stop of mud-brick and rope-strung awnings around the only sweet water for three days in any direction. By day it trades in salt, dates, and rumor; by night its doors are barred, because the hills sing and nobody stays outdoors to listen.
town_services: The shrine of the Weighing offers healing and honest burial at temple rates.
Dried rations, torches, oil, rope, and pack gear are sold in the caravan market.
Sef the scribe copies maps and buys tomb writings; Mother Herit hears oaths and confessions.

areas.name: Vestibule of the Sun Door
areas.description: Drifted sand fans across a floor of cracked gypsum tiles. The walls hold a painted procession of mourners whose faces have been chiselled away, every one, down to the plaster. Over the inner arch, a single line of glyphs survives; weathered as it is, the sign for 'dawn' repeats three times.

areas.name: Hall of Offerings
areas.description: Low stone tables line the walls, set with bowls, jars, and platters for a feast three hundred years stale. Everything edible is long since dust — and through the dust run fresh, small tracks in their hundreds.

areas.name: Processional of the Carriers
areas.description: A pillared hall where the funeral procession once formed up. Eight niches hold eight stone biers, and on four of them the honored dead still lie in wrappings gone the color of old paper. The wrappings are moving.

areas.name: The robbers' camp
areas.description: A cold camp in a corridor alcove: two bedrolls, a dead lantern, a scatter of date stones, and a game of knucklebones abandoned mid-throw. One bedroll is still occupied by its owner's boots. Nothing else of the owner remains.

areas.name: Chapel of the First Dawn
areas.description: The ceiling of this chapel is plastered midnight blue and set with gold-leaf stars; on the east wall, a painted sun crests painted hills. Below it stands a basalt altar, and webbing sheets the ceiling stars like cloud. On the altar rests a bronze disc with rays, no larger than a splayed hand — the sun taken down from its sky.

areas.name: Hall of the Weighing
areas.description: The grandest room of the upper tomb: a seven-pillar hall whose west wall carries a mural of the Weighing — a heart on one scale-pan, a feather on the other, and a queue of the dead awaiting the verdict. High among the pillars hang leathery shapes the size of waterskins, stirring at the light.

areas.name: The embalmers' cell
areas.description: Stone benches, copper hooks, and shelves of natron jars: the room where the honored dead were made ready. The floor slopes to a drain, and a track of polished wear crosses the threshold — the path of something heavy, swung often.

areas.name: The servants' hall
areas.description: Sleeping shelves in tiers, a cold hearth, and a long table set for a meal no one living was meant to eat. Three of the household dead stand at their places, waiting, wrapped hands folded.

areas.name: The false tomb
areas.description: A burial chamber in miniature: painted walls, a modest stone sarcophagus, grave-goods arranged just so. It is staged — the paint is thinner here, the offerings are plaster fakes, and the sarcophagus lid has been made easy to shift. Everything about the room invites a robber to be satisfied and leave.

areas.name: Hall of the Watchers
areas.description: Six full-harness soldiers of the old dynasty stand in wall niches flanking the way south, spears grounded, sockets forward. The dust on their shoulders is thick; the dust on their spear-blades is not.

areas.name: The descending way
areas.description: The corridor narrows and begins to slope, cut deeper and truer than everything above it. The air warms with every step down, dry as an oven, and carries a smell of hot resin. On the walls, the sun-glyph repeats at eye height, over and over, like a word said until it loses meaning.

areas.name: Shrine of the Vulture
areas.description: A small shrine to the carrion-mother, she who takes the flesh so the name may last. Her basalt image spreads chipped wings over an offering bowl. The kindly-faced old goddess has been re-painted at some point — recently, in lamp-soot black — so that her painted eyes look toward the south. Toward the vault.

areas.name: crypt
areas.description: the skeleton is here

features.description: Among the gnawed platters, three offering bowls of hammered silver still hold their tribute: a spill of tarnished coins fused by age into brittle clumps.
The grave-goods of the honored dead lie beneath the biers in cedar boxes gone soft with age: coin-silver by the handful and two carnelians cut in the old flat style.
A grave-robber's satchel, dropped in a hurry beside the bedrolls. It holds a pried-loose hoard of coins, a coil of good rope, and a crowbar with a bent claw.

The bronze sun-seal lifts from a shallow socket in the altar top. In a hollow beneath it lie the dawn-priests' vestments: a gilded vulture pectoral on a chain, and a purse of electrum struck with the erased king's profile.
The western alcove was bricked up and broken open again long ago. Behind the broken course, a tithe-chest holds temple silver and a moonstone the size of a thumbnail.

Four canopic jars stand in a wall niche, stoppered with wax. Three hold gems bedded in resin — payment sealed in with the organs, after the old custom. The fourth jar's lacquered clasp glints with something brighter than varnish.
Under the head servant's shelf, a strongbox of copper-banded acacia holds the household purse: the wages of the dead, counted and never spent.

The sarcophagus holds a wax-and-linen king with a gilt-bronze crown on its brow — and, tucked beneath the false body like an afterthought, a slab of real silver coin and a funerary tablet dense with chiselled glyphs, its royal name intact.
The offering bowl holds a drift of silver left coin by coin over generations, green-black with age.

dungeons.name: The House of the Second Dawn

journal.text: The party crosses out of the sun and into the House of the Second Dawn. The air inside is dry as paper and faintly warm, and from somewhere far below comes a sound on the very edge of hearing — a thin keening, like wind over a bottle's mouth, from a place where no wind is.
Mother Herit's charge stands: go down into the House of the Second Dawn, find what sings beneath the hills, and still it. The temple's silver — and the town's sleep — ride on it.

quests.name: The singing hills
quests.narrative: Mother Herit's charge stands: go down into the House of the Second Dawn, find what sings beneath the hills, and still it. The temple's silver — and the town's sleep — ride on it.
quests.speaker: Mother Herit

objectives.name: Still the voice beneath the hills
Recover a tomb writing that keeps the erased king's name
Bring the writing to Sef the scribe in Last Well

dungeons.name: The House of the Second Dawn

narrative.refusal: The bronze doors carry no handle and no keyhole — only a socket in the shape of a rayed sun, worn smooth at the edges by hands long turned to dust. Nothing the party carries fits it, and the doors stand as still as the hill above.
narrative.success: The sun-seal settles into the socket with a click like a jaw closing. Counterweights shift somewhere in the stone, and the bronze doors swing inward on three centuries of held breath.

features.description: The defacement is old and deliberate: each mourner's face was struck off with a chisel, and the same chisel-work erased a royal cartouche above the arch. Whoever did it worked from a ladder and took their time. The southern door of the vestibule is iron-bound and locked; its twin to the east hangs ajar.

effect.manual: The false king exhales: bitter yellow embalmers' gas fills the chamber when the lid shifts.

areas.name: Hall of the Watchers
areas.description: Six full-harness soldiers of the old dynasty stand in wall niches flanking the way south, spears grounded, sockets forward. The dust on their shoulders is thick; the dust on their spear-blades is not.

features.description: The niches are engineered: raised sills keep the watchers' feet clear of drifting sand, and a chiselled sight-line channel in each niche floor points at the door. This post was built to be stood forever.

areas.description: The corridor narrows and begins to slope, cut deeper and truer than everything above it. The air warms with every step down, dry as an oven, and carries a smell of hot resin. On the walls, the sun-glyph repeats at eye height, over and over, like a word said until it loses meaning.

areas.name: Vault of the Second Dawn
areas.description: The burial vault of Ozrum the Deathless. A false sky of gold leaf covers the ceiling, and against the east wall leans the work of three hundred years: a rising sun built from every scrap of gold, brass, and polished bronze the tomb could give up, lamp-lit from behind so it burns. Before it, on the king's bier, the royal husk lies under a shroud of stitched prayer-cloth. A gaunt figure in a vizier's cap turns from tending the lamps, and its dry voice cracks with joy: the guests have come, and the dawn is nearly ready.

features.description: The king's grave-goods are heaped about the bier as the old rites demand: chests of coin, the gold grave-mask that was to greet the dawn, twin suns of cut citrine — and the Crown of the Second Dawn itself, resting on the shrouded brow, waiting for the light.

areas.name: Gallery of the Nine Kings
areas.description: Nine seated basalt kings line this gallery, each with a name-tablet at its feet — eight names, worn but legible. The ninth king's face is chiselled smooth and his tablet is blank. Something glistens on the ceiling above the eighth, catching the torchlight the way water does, though nothing here has been wet for centuries.

features.description: The ninth king's erasure was done by the same chisel-hand as the vestibule frieze — and then, much later, someone gouged a single glyph into the blank tablet with a knife point: the sign for 'dawn'.
The eighth king alone keeps his eyes: two chalcedony ovals bedded in bitumen, loose enough to pry free.

areas.name: Shrine of the Vulture
areas.description: A small shrine to the carrion-mother, she who takes the flesh so the name may last. Her basalt image spreads chipped wings over an offering bowl. The kindly-faced old goddess has been re-painted at some point — recently, in lamp-soot black — so that her painted eyes look toward the south. Toward the vault.

features.description: The offering bowl holds a drift of silver left coin by coin over generations, green-black with age.

areas.name: Treasury of the Moulted Feather
areas.description: The tomb's working treasury, iron-doored and stacked with tribute chests, each lid painted with a single vulture feather — the sign of wealth given over to the dead. The topmost chest sits slightly proud of its stack, as if placed to be opened first.

features.description: Beneath the baited top chest, the true tribute: sacks of coin gone stiff with age, a collar of gold vulture feathers, and an uncut yellow sapphire wrapped in lead foil.

effect.manual: A scythe-blade sweeps hip-high from a slot in the chest stack when the top chest's lid lifts.

table.label: House of the Second Dawn, upper tomb

levels.guidance: A sealed royal tomb, desert-dry and pitch black: every sound is too loud and every torch is a violation. The dead here were servants once and remember service, not malice. The deeper the party goes, the warmer and closer the air becomes, as if the stone is holding its breath before a sunrise. Speak of dust, gold-leaf, bitumen, and the smell of old resin; never let the tomb feel looted or familiar.
